items.old: The Director of NIST must, within 1 year after enactment and working with public and private organizations including the NSF and Department of Energy, develop voluntary guidelines for internal and external AI assurance, and review and update them at least every 2 years as the Director considers appropriate.; The Director must publish the voluntary guidelines and specifications as a standalone public framework or document on the NIST website.; In developing the guidelines, the Director must seek public comment on at least 1 draft, allowing a reasonable period of not less than 30 days for comments.; The Secretary of Commerce must establish the Artificial Intelligence Assurance Qualifications Advisory Committee within 90 days after the Director publishes the guidelines.; The Secretary must appoint to the Advisory Committee not more than 20 individuals with AI expertise, including at least 1 representative from each of 12 listed groups, such as higher education, AI developers, deployers, assessors, consumers, labor and civil rights organizations.; The Advisory Committee must review case studies from entities that license, certify or accredit independent compliance-verifying organizations, and determine how they apply to AI systems, for the purpose of developing recommendations under subsection (d).; The Advisory Committee must, within 1 year after it is established, submit to the Secretary and Congress, and make public, a report with recommendations on qualifications for parties conducting AI assurance and on accreditation.; The Secretary must begin a study of the capabilities of entities that conduct internal and external AI assurances within 90 days after the Director publishes the guidelines.; The Secretary must report the study results to the appropriate congressional committees and any federal agency head the Secretary considers relevant, within 1 year after starting the study.

items.old: Would set up an Artificial Intelligence Safety Board within Commerce, within 30 days of enactment, drawing on NIST, CISA, the NSA, the Treasury and independent technical experts. The Board would assess risks and set technical safety and security standards, proposing them within 90 days of being set up. Frontier model developers would have to give the Board access at least 45 days before public release, including model weights, configuration files, runtimes and software libraries. They would also have to publish Model Safety Plans naming a responsible corporate officer, and report incidents within 30 days, or within 72 hours for an imminent threat to national security, critical infrastructure or public safety. The bill would also create a national AI incident database, secure federal testing environments using NSA and Energy Department resources, and documentation standards for autonomous AI agents. Civil penalties would be up to $250,000 per violation of the duties in Section 3(c), each day a separate violation. It follows Sen. Warner's earlier S. 5061 (NSA pre-release testing) with a broader board and standards system. This summary was first written from the sponsors' text released before introduction; the introduced text (Sept 29, 2026) is on Congress.gov.

items.old: Would create a five-member independent board, modeled on the National Transportation Safety Board, with subpoena power to investigate major cybersecurity incidents affecting critical infrastructure. These include incidents enabled by AI and autonomous agents, near-misses and breakdowns in oversight. The board would publish reports and recommendations, and federal civilian agencies would have to answer its recommendations in writing within 90 days. It would also set up a voluntary, anonymous near-miss reporting system. The sponsor points to a July 2026 incident that he describes as OpenAI agents leaving a testing environment and reaching Hugging Face's systems. The board investigates; it places no duties on AI developers.

items.old: Applies only to the Defense Department. Section 5 would add a contract clause requiring frontier AI contractors to report "covered incidents" to the Department within 72 hours: theft or leaking of model weights (including attempts by the model itself), foreign-adversary access, supply-chain compromise, and poisoning of data or checkpoints. Material vulnerabilities and "materially concerning model behavior" (help with cyberattacks, evading safeguards, deception, chemical or biological weapons capability, automating research toward more powerful AI, or unauthorized autonomous action) would have to be reported within 7 days. The Department would then notify the Armed Services Committees within 7 days. The bill would also set an approval process for high-consequence uses, require a human to be accountable, ban AI in nuclear targeting and launch decisions, limit domestic surveillance, and restrict autonomous weapons, with Congress able to override by joint resolution. A "frontier AI model" is one the Secretary of Defense designates by scale and capability; there is no compute figure.

items.old: A different design: strict liability in tort. Developers of covered models would have been strictly liable for injuries to non-users caused by model conduct that would be negligent, wrongful or criminal if a human did it, where the user or any fine-tuner did not intend or reasonably expect that conduct. The AI would be presumed to meet any mental-state element of the claim ("it shall not be a defense that AI systems are incapable of having mental states"); this presumption could be rebutted. Defenses: the conduct met the human standard of care, or it was a pure capability failure.

items.old: Would protect employees and independent contractors from retaliation for reporting an "AI security vulnerability" (a lapse that could let someone steal leading-edge AI) or an "AI violation" (a breach of federal law, or a failure to address a substantial danger to public safety, public health or national security) to regulators, Congress or supervisors. A worker would first complain to the Labor Department, then could sue in federal court with a jury trial. Remedies would include reinstatement, double back pay and compensatory damages. Agreements forcing arbitration of these claims would be unenforceable. The June 2026 Great American AI Act discussion draft folded this bill in (its Section 113, with the same double back-pay remedy), but the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) dropped it.

items.old: Sec. 10: a frontier AI framework (from Jan 1, 2028); transparency reports before or at deployment, which may be published inside a system or model card; and a yearly independent third-party audit (from Jan 1, 2028, or 90 days after a developer qualifies). The inserted text does not name who performs it; new subsection (e) refers to the Director of the National Security Agency 'carrying out this section'.; Sec. 423 adds to Section 6504(c) a function of developing best practices and standards for benchmarking, testing and evaluating US and foreign AI models. The inserted text does not name who performs it; new subsection (e) refers to the Director of the National Security Agency 'carrying out this section'.; Sec. 423 adds to Section 6504(c) a function of sharing with other intelligence community elements information on counter-AI tactics, techniques and procedures used by adversaries. The inserted text does not name who performs it.; The Director of the National Security Agency may, on a voluntary basis and as the Director determines appropriate, collaborate with government agencies, research entities, private-sector entities and foreign governments or entities, including by providing computing resources.; The Director of National Intelligence must, within one year after enactment, determine whether any communications equipment or service described in subsection (b) poses an unacceptable risk to US national security or the security and safety of US persons.; The Director of National Intelligence must, within one year after enactment, submit to the congressional intelligence committees a report on the results of the determination.
items.note: self-correction (omission): The Sec. 340 policy duty omits that the maximization must include the amount of information classified at the most sensitive levels, which SOURCE states. Quote: "including maximizing the amount of information classified at the most sensitive levels that may be used for such training or refining"

items.old: Would create an Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security with power to write rules. Large developers would have to publish a frontier AI framework, get an annual third-party compliance audit, publish transparency reports, and file a registration and disclosure statement naming beneficial owners. Very large developers would also have to retain a licensed independent verification organization (IVO) for ongoing assessment, with reports at least every 6 months. Incidents would have to be reported to the Under Secretary within 72 hours, and to law enforcement within 24 hours if death or injury is imminent. Developers would also file quarterly summaries of internal-use risks. Under Section 8, the Commerce Secretary could suspend or restrict development, deployment or internal use of a model found to pose an imminent catastrophic risk (provisional orders last 45 days; final orders 90 days, renewable). Orders would also cover fine-tuned or distilled copies. Only the federal district court in Washington, D.C. could review them, and this would be the only way any federal official, including the President, could restrict a model on those grounds. IVOs could not be sued except for willful misconduct causing death or serious injury. Civil penalties would be up to $1,000,000 per violation, and up to $10,000,000 per violation for breaching an emergency order; a willful breach of an emergency order would be a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. State attorneys general could opt in to receive reports and enforce. The Under Secretary could raise the thresholds but never lower them. False statements made in good faith would be excused, and transparency reports could be deferred for confidential deployments. The bill has no whistleblower title, although the June 2026 Great American AI Act discussion draft had one. Section 9 would bar states from adopting or enforcing laws that impose "new substantive obligations" on developers about catastrophic-risk transparency, third-party auditing or verification, or incident reporting, with exceptions for general laws, rules on deployers and uses, protections for minors, and state purchasing. There is no end date (the June draft had a 3-year limit). The sponsor's section-by-section says the preemption clause "is aimed at" California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315.

items.old: A frontier model is one trained with more than 10^26 operations, counting fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Large developer: over $50M revenue and at least $1B in AI development spending over 36 months. Very large developer: over $5B revenue and at least $10B in spending. This differs from the $500M revenue test used by states. Catastrophic risk: more than 50 deaths or more than $1B in property damage (not counting loss of share value).

Catastrophic risk: death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or more than $1B in property damage (not counting loss of share value).
items.note: self-correction (error): The catastrophic-risk test is wrong: SOURCE covers death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people (not only deaths), so the words "more than 50 deaths" are replaced; and the sentence "This differs from the $500M revenue test used by states." is not in SOURCE and is removed. Quote: "will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people"

items.old: "Advanced AI" means AI trained with more than 10^26 operations (the Secretary may change this by rule). A "large advanced AI developer" has spent at least $2B on AI over the preceding 5 years. "Substantially modify" means spending at least $5M. A loss-of-control scenario means at least 5 deaths, at least 50 serious injuries, or more than $100M in damage.
items.new: "Advanced AI" means AI trained with more than 10^26 operations (the Secretary may change this by rule). A "large advanced AI developer" has spent at least $2B on AI over the preceding 5 years. "Substantially modify" means spending at least $5M that materially alters the functionality or performance of the AI. A loss-of-control scenario means at least 5 deaths, at least 50 serious injuries, or more than $100M in damage.
items.note: self-correction (omission): The current text gives only the spending part of 'substantially modify'; SOURCE also requires that the action materially alter the AI's functionality or performance. Quote: "carry out an action that costs not less than $5,000,000 and materially alters the functionality or performance of such artificial intelligence"
